words.etymon: bʰuH- (mapping; Earth-word itself not cognate with Γαῖα)

cognate: *méh₂tēr 'mother' + *meǵh₂- 'great' (Gk μήτηρ μεγίστη ~ Ved. mātáraṃ mahī́m / mātā́ ... mahī́) as the title of Earth (or Aditi identified with Earth).
drift_or_renewal: The noun for Earth is renewed on both sides (Gk Γῆ; Ved. pr̥thivī́, bhū́mi, or Aditi); Greek has the superlative μεγίστη where Vedic has the positive mahī́. Greek adds a genitive of the gods (δαιμόνων Ὀλυμπίων), which matches Ved. mahī́m ... mātáraṃ suvratā́nām (AVŚ 7.6, support) in structure but not in wording.
shared_syntax: Appositive title: mother + 'great' (adjective agreeing with it) + the divine name of Earth, in the nominative or accusative of an invocation; optionally with a genitive plural naming the divine children.
context: Hymnic invocation of Earth as a divine mother. Solon (fr. 36, quoted in Ath. Pol. 12.4) calls on Earth as witness 'in the court of Time': 'greatest mother of the Olympian gods, best, black Earth'. In AVŚ 7.6 Aditi is invoked as 'the great mother' who holds the wide atmosphere in her lap, i.e. as Earth. In RV 1.72.9 'Earth spread out greatly with the great ones, the mother Aditi with her sons', and RV 1.164.33 / AVŚ 9.10.23 say 'my mother is this great earth'. AVŚ 12.1.12 says 'Earth is mother, I am the son of Earth'. The match is wording, not just a concept: the same cognate adjective is attached to the same cognate kin-term for the same referent, in a prayer register. But mother-Earth is close to universal and 'great' is a common epithet, so chance convergence cannot be ruled out.

cognate: *yewg- 'yoke' with *gʷṓws 'ox' as object (Gk ζεύγνυμι βοῦς ~ Lat. (con)iungere boues ~ Ved. yuj- gā́ḥ), in a ploughing frame; Gk and Lat also share *h₂érh₃trom 'plough' (ὑπέζευξε ἀρότρῳ βοῦν ~ boues ... aratrum; aratra ... iuga ... bubus).
drift_or_renewal: Vedic renews the plough word (lā́ṅgala-, sī́ra-; AVŚ 3.17.1 sīrā yuñjanti yokes the plough rather than the ox). The ox is renewed as vāhá- 'draught animal' in the Paippalāda ploughing charm (śunaṃ vāhasya yuktasya), though the RV keeps gā́ḥ with yuj- (RV 1.84.16, 1.151.4, 10.27.20).
shared_syntax: Transitive verb of yoking + accusative 'ox/oxen' (Gk, Lat, Ved). In Gk the dative of the implement (ἀρότρῳ) is the 'to which' complement, as Ved. dhurí ('to the pole') is in RV 1.84.16 / 1.151.4.
context: Agricultural ploughing. Demades describes man's mastery of animals: he 'yoked the ox to the plough for working the land'. Cato lists ploughs, yokes and ox harness, says three oxen in tandem draw one plough, and says oxen may be yoked on holy days (138.1). The Paippalāda charm (= RV 4.57.4 type: śunaṃ vāhāḥ ... śunam aṣṭrām) wishes luck to the yoked draught-ox and the goad. The congruence is real, but this is technical vocabulary for an inherited technology rather than a poetic figure: once the words for yoke and ox are inherited, the collocation follows almost necessarily. So it is evidence of inherited agricultural phraseology at best.
